title: Khonani

jokes.text: Did you know that everybody here went out last night without us? Oh, nerds!
jokes.setup: Liz discovers the staff went out without her and Jack
jokes.punchline: She calls them 'nerds' — a mild, childish insult that reveals her own social awkwardness
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Liz calling her staff 'nerds' for socializing exposes her own nerdiness — she's the one who feels left out. It's a quick, efficient character beat. Not exceptional but perfectly calibrated to Liz's voice.

jokes.text: 'Well, I yelled "baba booey" at Walter Cronkite's funeral, so I actually have no idea what's rude or not.'
jokes.setup: Liz complains that not being invited to Thursday Night Thunder is rude
jokes.punchline: Tracy deflects with a completely unhinged confession about yelling a Howard Stern catchphrase at a national icon's funeral, presented as disqualifying him from judging rudeness
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect Tracy Jordan joke. The specificity of 'Walter Cronkite's funeral' (a revered figure) + 'baba booey' (juvenile shock-jock catchphrase) creates a perfect collision of registers. It's deeply character-specific — only Tracy would say this, and the logic ('so I have no idea what's rude') is perfectly absurd. Highly quotable. Earns its 8+ easily.

jokes.text: Tracy asks Liz to take care of Angie 'like a husband until this whole ass-ache blows over'
jokes.setup: Tracy's wife Angie is on bed rest and needs care; Tracy asks Liz if there's anything she can do
jokes.punchline: Tracy's request is 'take care of Angie like a husband' — implying he himself can't or won't do it, and the phrasing 'ass-ache' for a medical pregnancy complication
jokes.explanation: Strong character comedy — Tracy's casual abdication of husband duties framed as a reasonable ask is very on-brand. 'Ass-ache' as descriptor for pregnancy complications is a nice touch of Tracy's vernacular.

jokes.text: 'I haven't seen your brow that furrowed since you saw that picture of Helen Mirren in a bikini. How is it possible? Is she a wizard?'
jokes.setup: Liz notices Jack looking troubled and tries to identify what's bothering him
jokes.punchline: The reference is to Jack being baffled/disturbed by Helen Mirren's attractiveness in a bikini — and Liz has apparently witnessed this specific reaction before. 'Is she a wizard?' is Jack's genuine confusion framed as the punchline.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully constructed. The Helen Mirren bikini reference is specific enough to be surprising, Jack's confused attraction framed as existential ('Is she a wizard?') is perfectly in character for a man who reduces everything to power dynamics. The non sequitur 'A question for another time, Lemon' dismissal is also funny. Strong character specificity.

jokes.text: I was about to say 'oh, Nancy' but stopped myself — 'Oh, Nan... Na... Nana. Have I not told you about my grandmother fetish?'
jokes.setup: Jack almost calls out Nancy's name mid-thought with Avery present; starts to say 'Nancy' then pivots desperately
jokes.punchline: He lands on 'Nana' and invents a grandmother fetish on the spot as cover — an absurd save that creates a second level of awkwardness
jokes.explanation: Strong structural misdirection — the joke works in layers. First, Jack nearly slips. Then his cover story (grandmother fetish) is more outrageous than the original problem. The beat where Liz has to compute what he's saying adds a nice reaction layer.

jokes.text: Avery put mothballs behind her ears and fed Jack peppermints to lean into the grandmother fetish
jokes.setup: Jack has claimed a grandmother fetish to cover for almost saying Nancy's name
jokes.punchline: Avery, being the ultra-competitive overachiever she is, immediately adopted the grandmother roleplay: mothballs behind ears + peppermints. 'She is in it to win it.'
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'grandmother fetish' to specific sensory details (mothballs = smell, peppermints = taste) is inspired. 'She is in it to win it' as the payoff perfectly captures Avery's character while making the absurdity land harder. The specificity of the grandmother props elevates this from a solid joke to an excellent one. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Jack lists past 'tough decisions': switching Sheinhardt's wig production to 100% Chinese cadaver hair, turning down Dick Cheney's offer to become King of Iraq, and selecting the new NBC logo
jokes.setup: Jack claims the Nancy/Avery decision is the toughest he's ever had to make, listing past tough calls for comparison
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from corporate malfeasance (cadaver hair) to geopolitical absurdity (King of Iraq) to the deflating anti-climax of the NBC logo — each item funnier than the last, with the logo being the joke within the joke
jokes.explanation: Classic 30 Rock list comedy. The escalation structure is perfect: first item is darkly corporate, second is geopolitically insane, third is the comedically deflating non-sequitur. The specificity of 'Chinese cadaver hair' and 'King of Iraq' are both memorably absurd. The NBC logo punchline also sets up the next joke. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: [NBC chime plays] followed by Jack saying 'It's fresh.'
jokes.setup: Jack has just said selecting the NBC logo was one of his toughest decisions
jokes.punchline: The NBC chime plays and Jack says 'It's fresh' — deadpan self-congratulation for what is clearly a mediocre/embarrassing choice
jokes.explanation: A running gag that works on multiple levels: NBC's self-parody, Jack's unearned confidence, and the chime as a punchline delivery mechanism. 'It's fresh' as the total defense of a logo is very funny in its breezy corporate emptiness.

jokes.text: Liz says 'sometimes when you try so hard to find love, you can't see that it's been standing in front of you the whole time' — implying she and Jack should be together — and Jack says 'Oh, good God' and starts laughing
jokes.setup: Liz is ostensibly giving Jack advice about his Nancy/Avery dilemma
jokes.punchline: The subtext is clearly Liz suggesting she and Jack are meant for each other; Jack's 'Oh, good God' + laughter is the punchline — the show knows the audience might expect this and explicitly rejects it
jokes.explanation: Meta-subversive: the show teases a romantic cliché and then immediately mocks it. Jack's genuine laughter is the right reaction. Works well as character comedy — both characters defined by the joke.

jokes.text: Kenneth tells Jack he's going to Mr. Jordan's house and will 'call when he gets there so you know I'm safe' — Jack snaps 'No! I don't care if you're safe! I love you!'
jokes.setup: Kenneth dutifully notifies Jack of his departure like a worried parent checking in
jokes.punchline: Jack's frustrated non-sequitur — 'I don't care if you're safe! I love you!' — is both a commentary on the Liz 'family' conversation and an absurd reversal of expected employer/employee dynamics
jokes.explanation: Jack's non-sequitur emotional outburst is funny and contextually loaded — he's just been talking about workplace family dynamics. The logic is scrambled in the right way.

jokes.text: Jack offers Liz a drink as a 'fellow manager' — she accepts — then immediately drops her glass
jokes.setup: Jack invites Liz to bond over drinks as a 'fellow manager' — a condescending gesture disguised as friendship
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately drops her glass, undercutting any attempt at dignified peer bonding
jokes.explanation: A functional visual gag that reinforces Liz's awkwardness. Not the most original beat but serves character efficiently.

jokes.text: 'Is that supposed to be a broom? Anchor the handle. / Yeah. / There it is.'
jokes.setup: Liz has dropped her glass and is apparently trying to clean it up with something inadequate
jokes.punchline: Jack's coaching of Liz on basic broom technique — 'anchor the handle,' 'there it is' — as if she were learning a complex skill, played completely straight
jokes.explanation: Jack's deadpan coaching of a basic task is perfectly in character — he relates to everyone as a subordinate needing guidance. The measured pacing ('Yeah. / There it is.') makes it funnier than it reads on the page.

jokes.text: Tracy answers his phone: 'This better be important. I'm in a meeting.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth calls Tracy, presumably at home taking care of Angie
jokes.punchline: Tracy uses the corporate 'I'm in a meeting' deflection despite obviously not being in any meeting — pure Tracy delusion about his own importance
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy. Not surprising but lands because it's so perfectly Tracy.

jokes.text: Tracy says he couldn't understand his wedding vows because 'Rick James was officiating and I couldn't really understand anything Rick James was saying'
jokes.setup: Kenneth reminds Tracy of his wedding vows — 'in sickness and in health'
jokes.punchline: Tracy claims Rick James officiated the wedding and was incomprehensible, as a non-excuse for not knowing his own vows
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character specificity. Only Tracy Jordan would have had Rick James marry him. The logic is Tracy-perfect: he didn't understand the vows not because he wasn't paying attention but because Rick James was mumbling. The celebrity name is earned — it tells us something true about Tracy's world. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Tracy offers Kenneth free food from the fridge and then says 'once I'm there, I'll determine how much to charge you'
jokes.setup: Tracy is reluctantly agreeing to come home; he tells Kenneth he can eat from the fridge
jokes.punchline: The immediate pivot to charging Kenneth for the food he just offered, as if he's running a hospitality business
jokes.explanation: Solid Tracy absurdism — the transactional attitude toward his own employee/friend is characteristic. The non-sequitur pivot from generosity to billing is the joke.

jokes.text: Frank claims he had a 'doctor's appointment' instead of admitting he went to Thursday Night Thunder — then immediately screams about the underside of an octopus
jokes.setup: Liz asks Frank what he did last night, knowing he was at Thursday Night Thunder
jokes.punchline: Frank tries to claim a doctor's appointment, then is distracted by something horrifying (implied: a rash or growth he's showing) — 'Oh, God, it looks like the underside of an octopus!'
jokes.explanation: The cutaway implies Frank showing something medically disturbing at his doctor's appointment — the 'underside of an octopus' description is memorably disgusting and specific. The structure is good: awkward lie → horrifying visual reveal. The line itself is very quotable.

jokes.text: Jenna asks to speak to Liz in 'the office where everyone clips their toenails' — Liz says 'Not cool, guys.'
jokes.setup: Jenna wants a private word with Liz
jokes.punchline: The room is identified by the specific gross habit performed there — implying a real, established problem — and Liz's resigned 'not cool, guys' confirms it's a real ongoing issue
jokes.explanation: Very efficient world-building comedy. The room being identified by toenail clipping rather than any functional name tells you everything about TGS's workplace culture. Liz's weary acceptance ('Not cool, guys') is perfectly in character.

jokes.text: Cerie's fiancé was captured by pirates on his dad's yacht but was rescued 'thanks to the A-Team' — and 'he has a different energy now. He's quieter.'
jokes.setup: Cerie explains why the wedding was off for a while
jokes.punchline: The A-Team rescued him from pirates, delivered with total deadpan sincerity, and the haunted 'he has a different energy now. He's quieter.' implies PTSD from a cartoon adventure
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The A-Team reference is absurd but the real laugh is 'he has a different energy now. He's quieter.' — which implies genuine trauma from a ridiculous scenario. The deadpan delivery of existential crisis caused by a pop-culture reference is 30 Rock at its finest. Highly quotable. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: 'He has a different energy now. He's quieter.' — Cerie describing her post-pirate-captivity fiancé as if he's had a mild personality shift
jokes.setup: Cerie explains her fiancé is recovering from being held captive by pirates
jokes.punchline: Her assessment — 'He has a different energy now. He's quieter.' — is such a grotesque understatement of pirate-induced PTSD that it's darkly funny
jokes.explanation: Extremely economical dark comedy. Cerie's total obliviousness to what pirate captivity does to a person is a perfect character beat — her shallowness turns a traumatic event into a mild observation. 'He's quieter' as the sum total of her concern is quietly devastating and very funny.

jokes.text: 'You're gonna be so out of place, Liz.'
jokes.setup: Cerie has just listed her bridesmaids — beautiful, glamorous, celebrity-adjacent
jokes.punchline: Jenna's blunt, casual statement that Liz will be out of place among them — delivered as statement of fact, not insult
jokes.explanation: Quick, efficient character beat. Jenna's oblivious cruelty-as-observation is consistent with her character. Economy is the main virtue here.

jokes.text: Cerie says the schedule is filling up 'now that Aris is finally getting over his Stockholm syndrome'
jokes.setup: Cerie explains why the party needs to happen this week
jokes.punchline: Stockholm syndrome — identifying with his captors — mentioned as a scheduling inconvenience, not a serious trauma, while Cerie remains completely unbothered
jokes.explanation: The callback deepens joke #18. 'Stockholm syndrome' framed as a scheduling obstacle is a perfect extension of the absurdist premise. Cerie's total indifference to her fiancé's psychological trauma is very funny.

jokes.text: 'You guys may have to walk down the aisle with some pirates.'
jokes.setup: Cerie is explaining wedding logistics
jokes.punchline: Pirates as wedding party members, delivered as a minor logistical note
jokes.explanation: The escalating pirate thread gets one more beat — walking down the aisle with pirates — and the casual delivery makes it land. Part of a running absurdist gag that builds well across the scene.

jokes.text: Liz says she's too grouchy from a juice fast to plan the party — then immediately announces she'll throw the party tonight to prove she's fun
jokes.setup: Liz says the juice fast makes her too grouchy to plan anything
jokes.punchline: In the next breath, she announces a party to prove she's fun — the juice fast grouchiness immediately manifesting in the irrational decision she's making
jokes.explanation: Character-perfect irony: Liz proves she's not fun by her aggressive, resentful declaration that she will be fun. The self-awareness gap is the joke.

jokes.text: Liz raps: '* And there ain't no party / Like a Liz Lemon party / 'Cause a Liz Lemon party is mandatory *'
jokes.setup: Liz has just announced her revenge party with manic energy
jokes.punchline: The improvised rap explicitly tells everyone that attendance is mandatory — the complete antithesis of a fun party — proving the point that Liz cannot be fun
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a genuine 30 Rock classic. The rap structure (a fun form) is undermined by the word 'mandatory' — the most un-fun word possible — in the rhyme position. It's perfectly Liz: she is trying so hard to be fun that she makes fun mandatory, which is definitionally not fun. The word choice is exactly right. Economy is perfect. Quotability is very high. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: Jack reads from a self-help book: 'Hard Equations and Rational Thinking' — pauses — then says 'Damn you, heart.'
jokes.setup: Jack is 'in the bunker' trying to make a rational decision about Nancy vs. Avery using a book called 'Hard Equations and Rational Thinking'
jokes.punchline: 'Damn you, heart.' — after reading a book explicitly about rational thinking, Jack is defeated by emotion, framed as a dramatic battle with his own heart
jokes.explanation: Jack's relationship with his own emotions as an antagonist is perfectly in character. The pause between reading and the declaration makes it land. 'Damn you, heart' is delivered with total seriousness about something every human relates to. Earns its 8.

jokes.text: Jack apologizes for letting 'a Kashmiri into your office' — the janitor Khonani — as if it's a security breach
jokes.setup: Jack is interrupted in his bunker by the janitor Khonani who wants to discuss his promised promotion
jokes.punchline: Jonathan apologizes specifically for 'letting a Kashmiri' in — the geographic specificity of the insult framing an immigrant janitor as a diplomatic incident
jokes.explanation: The joke is the gap between corporate snobbery (security breach framing) and reality (a janitor with a legitimate grievance). Functional but not one of the episode's standouts.

jokes.text: Jack suddenly decides the janitor situation is the right time to 'stay deeply involved with subordinates' — immediately abandoning the Nancy/Avery decision
jokes.setup: Jack is supposed to be in the bunker making a tough personal decision; he's also just told Liz that bosses should stay distant from subordinates
jokes.punchline: The moment an actual problem arrives, Jack reverses his stated philosophy — and Liz previously said the same thing back to him — revealed as pure avoidance
jokes.explanation: The ironic reversal of Jack's stated philosophy is sharp. It works as both character comedy (Jack avoids emotional problems) and structural comedy (callback to the earlier advice).

jokes.text: Jack admits he promised Khonani the night shift because 'these immigrants have a tough life, no health care, and I kind of just thought he'd die before it became a thing'
jokes.setup: Liz asks why Jack would ever promise Khonani the earlier shift
jokes.punchline: Jack's reasoning: he felt guilty about immigrant hardship, so he made a promise he intended to never keep because he assumed the man would die first
jokes.explanation: One of the darkest and funniest Jack jokes in the episode. The construction is perfect: sympathetic gesture (I felt bad for immigrants) → corporate cynicism (I promised because he'd die) → delivered with complete matter-of-fact sincerity. This captures Jack Donaghy's character in one sentence — the simultaneous awareness of injustice and willingness to exploit it. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Jack explains his signature on the contract: 'In my defense, every April 22nd I honor Richard Nixon's death by getting drunk and making some unpopular decisions.'
jokes.setup: Khonani presents a contract that Jack clearly doesn't remember signing
jokes.punchline: Jack's alibi is that he ritually gets drunk every April 22nd to honor Richard Nixon's death by making bad decisions — a specific, absurd, and perfectly in-character explanation
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and a genuine 30 Rock classic. Every component works: (1) honoring Nixon specifically (not just 'a president,' but the most famous disgrace) (2) by getting drunk (the appropriate tribute) (3) and making unpopular decisions (Nixon's defining quality) (4) every year, ritually. This is an entire character biography compressed into one sentence. It's specific, quotable, and could only be Jack Donaghy. Comparable to the calibration anchors at the 8+ level. Strong 9.

jokes.text: [NBC chime plays] 'The Biggest Loser Network'
jokes.setup: Jack assures Khonani that NBC always keeps its promises
jokes.punchline: The NBC chime plays and Jack follows it with '...The Biggest Loser Network' — NBC's self-description is both a real show title and a brutal self-assessment
jokes.explanation: The NBC chime gag's best iteration. 'The Biggest Loser Network' works on two levels: the literal show title on NBC and the self-deprecating admission. This is 30 Rock's meta-NBC humor at its sharpest. The structure (solemn chime → devastating self-burn) is excellent.

jokes.text: Tracy has trained his dog Tracy Senior 'to hate white people because, not to profile, but most ghosts are white'
jokes.setup: Kenneth is attacked by Tracy's dog when arriving at his house
jokes.punchline: Tracy explains the dog was trained to hate white people — as a ghost deterrent, since ghosts are predominantly white — delivered with complete logical sincerity
jokes.explanation: The qualifier 'not to profile, but...' followed immediately by racial profiling is a perfect construction. The ghost logic — a genuine Tracy belief system — makes it absurdist rather than just a racial joke. Could only be Tracy. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Angie put up an invisible fence to keep Tracy's dog home because he 'would run away and cause car accidents and impregnate neighbors' horses'
jokes.setup: Tracy explains why the dog has an invisible fence
jokes.punchline: The three-part escalation: running away → causing car accidents → impregnating neighbors' horses. The final item in the list is absurdly specific and unexpected.
jokes.explanation: Classic rule-of-three escalation where the third item is deliberately impossible/absurd. 'Impregnate neighbors' horses' is specific enough to be genuinely surprising. The delivery implies Tracy finds this normal.

jokes.text: Tracy says his dog is trapped by the invisible fence 'just like me!' — drawing a parallel between his dog's captivity and his own marriage obligations
jokes.setup: Tracy is explaining the invisible fence and why the dog can't leave
jokes.punchline: Tracy identifies with the dog — trapped in the yard, can't escape — as a metaphor for feeling obligated to stay home with his sick wife
jokes.explanation: The man-dog parallel is a bit on-the-nose but Tracy's delivery of it with complete sincerity saves it. Not the strongest Tracy beat in the episode.

jokes.text: Kenneth tells Tracy his wife wants a PB&J sandwich. Tracy responds: 'No, we're not supposed to do any sex stuff while she's on bed rest. / Oh! Like a real one!'
jokes.setup: Kenneth says Angie has a craving for a peanut butter and jelly sandwich
jokes.punchline: Tracy immediately interprets 'PB&J' as a sexual euphemism, refuses on medical grounds, then is genuinely surprised it's just a real sandwich
jokes.explanation: Perfect Tracy misdirection. The joke is two-stage: first that Tracy has sexualized a PB&J (character-specific) and second that the reveal of it being a real sandwich is a surprise to him ('Oh! Like a real one!'). The construction is airtight. 'I'm on it!' immediately after is the button. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: 'Nope! I'm in a strip club! My bad!'
jokes.setup: Tracy has finally committed to making a sandwich and taking care of Angie, resolving to 'stay focused'
jokes.punchline: Immediate cut — Tracy has gone to a strip club instead of taking the sandwich to his wife. 'My bad!' as the response to a pregnant woman not receiving her medicine
jokes.explanation: Superb cutaway gag. The setup is Tracy's solemn commitment. The payoff is immediate, total failure. 'My bad!' as the excuse for abandoning a pregnant woman is peak Tracy casual irresponsibility. Economy is near-perfect — five words deliver everything. The rhythm of 'Nope! / I'm in a strip club! / My bad!' is a great comedic triple-beat. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Jenna thinks 'ice' means drugs because 'it's caused a lot of ODs in the porn community'
jokes.setup: Liz asks Jenna how much ice she should get for the party
jokes.punchline: Jenna assumes 'ice' is methamphetamine because of her specific experience in the porn industry, where it's apparently a known danger
jokes.explanation: Perfect Jenna Maroney joke. 'ODs in the porn community' is exactly the kind of specific, dark, world-building detail that makes 30 Rock's character comedy exceptional. The wordplay (ice = drugs) is earned because of character specificity.

jokes.text: Liz says she's dating Subhas the janitor — Jack says 'Lemon, please.' — Liz corrects him: 'No, it's not that. We're dating.'
jokes.setup: Jack mentions Subhas, the first-shift janitor; Liz says she 'kind of' knows him
jokes.punchline: Liz's clarification that she IS dating the janitor — after Jack assumes a different (presumably bathroom-related) connection — is the reversal, and Jack's 'Lemon, please' suggests he expected something even less dignified
jokes.explanation: The callback to Liz calling the janitor about home toilet situations is implied. 'Lemon, please' followed by the reveal that she's dating him — which is somehow the more surprising option — works well.

jokes.text: Liz scrolls for Subhas's phone number and Jack says 'I know you know it by heart' — Liz immediately rattles off '917...'
jokes.setup: Liz pretends to scroll for Subhas's number to maintain the pretense she doesn't know it by heart
jokes.punchline: Jack calls it out, and Liz immediately recites the area code without hesitation — the pretense collapses instantly
jokes.explanation: Quick, efficient character beat. The cut-off '917...' is funnier than any completed number would be. Good economy.

jokes.text: Khonani claims Subhas will want to leave to pursue his hobby of collecting 'classic car...' [coughs] 'cardboard. Classic cardboard.'
jokes.setup: Khonani assures Jack that Subhas will happily step aside for his hobbies
jokes.punchline: The mid-sentence cough obscures what was going to be 'classic cars' — revealing it's actually 'classic cardboard' — a collecting hobby appropriate for an underpaid janitor. The cough is doing narrative work.
jokes.explanation: Ingenious construction. The cough as a narrative device that drops economic class one tier mid-sentence is inventive. 'Classic cardboard' as a collection hobby tells you everything about Subhas's economic reality in two words. The word 'classic' doing double duty (car enthusiast vocabulary applied to trash) is genuine craft. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Tracy says: 'I'm like a chameleon, always a lizard.'
jokes.setup: Tracy acknowledges he can't change his irresponsible behavior ('I've been me for a long time')
jokes.punchline: The 'chameleon' metaphor implies adaptability, but Tracy's addition of 'always a lizard' reduces the metaphor to its literal base animal — he's using a metaphor for change to say he never changes, while also being technically wrong about chameleons
jokes.explanation: One of the great 30 Rock lines. Tracy's self-awareness-adjacent statement collapses the metaphor perfectly. A chameleon IS always a lizard — it's literally true — but saying so completely misses the point of the metaphor. It's simultaneously profound (he's saying he doesn't change at the core) and deeply stupid (he doesn't understand the metaphor). This double-layer of meaning is very rare. Comparable to the calibration anchors at 8+. Genuinely exceptional. Perfect economy — six words.

jokes.text: Liz wants Tracy to show 'the behavior that got you kicked out of the inaugural ball'
jokes.setup: Liz is begging Tracy to come to her party and be chaotic/fun
jokes.punchline: Tracy was kicked out of a presidential inaugural ball — and this behavior is now being requested for a work party
jokes.explanation: The implication of Tracy at a presidential inauguration is funny; being kicked out is better. Good character worldbuilding.

jokes.text: 'The secret service never gave me back my T-shirt cannon'
jokes.setup: Tracy explains why he can't do 'that behavior' at Liz's party
jokes.punchline: The Secret Service confiscated his T-shirt cannon at the inaugural ball — the specific prop implies exactly what chaos Tracy caused and why it was confiscated
jokes.explanation: Superb economy. The T-shirt cannon explains the inaugural ball incident without stating it. The Secret Service's involvement transforms what would be a minor party foul into a federal incident. 'Never gave me back' implies Tracy repeatedly asked for it. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Tracy tells Liz 'People don't say that anymore. They say "surf party, USA."'
jokes.setup: Liz asks Tracy to make the party 'off the hook'
jokes.punchline: Tracy corrects her slang — 'they say surf party, USA' — which is not a phrase anyone says, delivered with complete authority
jokes.explanation: Tracy confidently correcting someone's slang with complete nonsense is perfectly in character. 'Surf party, USA' sounds like an invented phrase from a different decade, delivered as current. Good economy.

jokes.text: Tracy delivers the frisbee/quarry metaphor: 'Parties are like frisbees. If you throw them the wrong way, they'll veer off in a bad direction, and then your kid will fall into a quarry.'
jokes.setup: Tracy is giving Liz advice about not throwing a revenge party
jokes.punchline: The frisbee metaphor starts reasonably (parties can go wrong) then veers into a specific disaster (child in quarry) that is both unexpected and presented as the logical conclusion
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Tracy moments. The frisbee metaphor is coherent until 'your kid will fall into a quarry' — which is both completely out of nowhere and presented as the natural consequence. It then gets a callback follow-up about the wife turning on you 'like your wife after your kid has fallen into a quarry' — implying Tracy has SPECIFIC experience with this scenario. The escalation from metaphor to implied personal tragedy is exceptional. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Tracy says his body 'is gonna take him to Liz Lemon's' despite his mind knowing he should stay — and the dog whines as if agreeing
jokes.setup: Tracy is torn between staying with Angie and going to Liz's party
jokes.punchline: Tracy frames his lack of self-control as his body literally overriding his brain — delivered as a genuine philosophical observation. The dog's whine is a visual/audio reaction beat.
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy. The body/mind split is an old joke but Tracy's sincerity makes it work. Dog reaction is a bonus beat.

jokes.text: Tracy puts the electric dog collar on himself and Kenneth says 'It would be my honor'
jokes.setup: Tracy needs to be physically prevented from going to Liz's party; he instructs Kenneth to put the electric dog collar on him
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's response — 'It would be my honor' — to the request to electrocute his boss whenever he tries to leave is delivered with complete earnestness
jokes.explanation: The callback to the invisible fence — now applied to Tracy himself — is excellent. Kenneth's enthusiastic honor at being assigned this task is perfect character comedy for both of them. The escalation of the dog subplot reaching its natural conclusion.

jokes.text: Subhas shows Jack his 'special book' — 'more men in it than I would have expected. Book is book.'
jokes.setup: Subhas has a 'special book' that the janitors keep, presumably containing headshots of people photographed in unflattering situations
jokes.punchline: Jack's observation that it contains 'more men than expected' — implying the contents are either embarrassing or erotic in nature — and Subhas's shrug: 'Book is book'
jokes.explanation: 'Book is book' is a perfect deadpan non-explanation. The implication of what the book contains is funnier than any explicit description. Good economy.

jokes.text: Jack announces he is 'innoventing' — 'a word that I just innovented'
jokes.setup: Jack says there's a way for everyone to get what they want and for him to look like 'a genius and a hero'
jokes.punchline: Jack coins the word 'innoventing' and immediately uses it again in his own definition — completely self-contained, self-validating logic
jokes.explanation: The recursive self-definition ('a word I just innovented') is beautifully constructed. Jack using his own new word in its own definition is both arrogant and logically self-defeating — perfect for his character. 'Innoventing' is a genuinely good portmanteau. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: [NBC chime plays] again — third instance, now after 'innoventing' solution
jokes.setup: Jack has 'solved' the janitor problem with his 'innovented' solution
jokes.punchline: The NBC chime plays again — now purely as Jack's personal theme/self-congratulation — the gag has escalated to Jack using the network's jingle as a personal victory sound
jokes.explanation: Third iteration of the running gag — diminishing returns but still functional. Without a subversive payoff this time, it's more of a punctuation mark than a joke.

jokes.text: Tracy Senior the dog 'took off fast. He did not want to live here.'
jokes.setup: The dog apparently escaped while they were talking
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's flat observation that the dog 'did not want to live here' — a completely matter-of-fact commentary on Tracy's household being unlivable even for a dog
jokes.explanation: Good deadpan button on the dog subplot. The implication that the Jordan household is so chaotic even the dog bolted is character-consistent.

jokes.text: Tracy's kids keep him out of the liquor cabinet by pouring glue in the lock
jokes.setup: Tracy needs a way to keep himself from removing the electric collar — Kenneth asks what will stop him
jokes.punchline: Tracy knows the method because his own children use it to keep him away from the liquor cabinet — the children are responsible for managing their father's alcoholism
jokes.explanation: Dark and excellent. The inversion — children parenting the parent — is Tracy's whole character in a single image. 'That's how my kids keep me out of the liquor cabinet' is delivered like a normal household tip.

jokes.text: Tracy tells Kenneth 'You're Tracy Jordan now.' — Kenneth responds 'Yes, sir! / Wait. I don't walk that well.'
jokes.setup: Tracy can't be in two places — at home and at Liz's party — so he sends Kenneth as his double
jokes.punchline: Kenneth immediately accepts being Tracy Jordan, then catches himself on the one specific detail he's not sure he can replicate: Tracy's walk
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. Kenneth's instant, enthusiastic acceptance of becoming another person — with zero hesitation — is perfectly Kenneth. The button ('I don't walk that well') implies Tracy's walk is uniquely difficult to replicate, which raises the question of what exactly it looks like. Good economy on the punchline.

jokes.text: Jack discovering there's no trash because Subhas takes it all — 'No trash left for Khonani'
jokes.setup: Jack's 'innovative' solution was to move Subhas to 10pm so both janitors could work; Khonani reports his first day
jokes.punchline: The unintended consequence of Jack's plan: Subhas at 10pm takes all the trash, leaving nothing for Khonani at 11:30 — the 'innovation' has made things worse
jokes.explanation: The logical failure of Jack's plan works as a plot joke that also mirrors the Nancy/Avery theme: you can't actually share, someone always loses. Functional but serves the larger story engine.

jokes.text: Jack breaks down: 'I'm the trash shift, Khonani. I'm the trash.'
jokes.setup: Khonani is explaining that two people can't share the same thing; Jack realizes this is exactly his Nancy/Avery situation
jokes.punchline: Jack's dramatic revelation that he is the 'trash' — the thing both Nancy and Avery want — delivered with total earnestness to a janitor
jokes.explanation: The structural payoff of the A and B plots intersecting. Jack Donaghy, one of TV's most powerful men, identifying himself as 'the trash' to a janitor is a great irony. The delivery is sincere — Jack doesn't recognize the absurdity — which makes it funnier. 'That sounds very difficult' from Khonani is the perfect understated response. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Khonani says he has a job at 'Fox...' [cough] 'Woods. Foxwoods casino. My cousin is head janitor there.'
jokes.setup: Khonani says he has another job option at Fox —
jokes.punchline: The cough obscures what sounded like 'Fox' (the rival network — a misdirect) and reveals 'Foxwoods casino.' The cough gag callback from the 'classic cardboard' joke works again.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the cough-as-narrative-device is smart. The Fox → Foxwoods misdirection is a nice touch — the audience expects a network rivalry joke but gets a casino. And Khonani's cousin being head janitor at Foxwoods completes his character nicely.

jokes.text: 'You ought to get that cough checked out.'
jokes.setup: Khonani has been coughing throughout the episode as a running gag
jokes.punchline: Jack's belated, casual medical advice to someone who may be seriously ill — delivered as an afterthought after firing him
jokes.explanation: The button on the Khonani cough gag. Jack's casual 'you ought to get that checked out' after denying this man his promised promotion is a perfect Jack Donaghy beat — technically caring while being completely tone-deaf. Good economy.

jokes.text: Tracy answers phone: 'This better be meetment, I'm importing.'
jokes.setup: Third iteration of Tracy's phone greeting gag — each one more scrambled than the last
jokes.punchline: 'Meetment' and 'importing' — Tracy has now completely garbled both words in the phrase he's been trying to deliver all episode
jokes.explanation: The third iteration of the phone greeting gag with maximum degradation — both words have now been corrupted into non-words. 'Meetment' and 'importing' are funnier than the previous versions. Good running gag escalation.

jokes.text: Kenneth forgot to get Angie's blood pressure medicine — 'I just didn't want to go outside! It's chilly!'
jokes.setup: Kenneth calls to say Angie's blood pressure medicine is in her car — parked outside the electric fence
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's reason for not getting it: he didn't want to go outside because it's chilly — a catastrophically irresponsible reason delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: The contrast between the medical urgency and Kenneth's trivial reason (chilly) is a clean character joke. Kenneth's oblivious goodness — he's apologizing while still not going out — is consistent.

jokes.text: Tracy tells Kenneth his dog may be hunting him and suggests: 'I suggest you cut off a finger and throw it in the river.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks if there's any chance Tracy's dog followed him to Liz's party
jokes.punchline: Tracy's practical advice for evading the hunting dog is to cut off a finger as a decoy — delivered as genuine tactical guidance, with complete calm
jokes.explanation: Tracy as tactical advisor gives genuinely dangerous advice with complete sincerity. The specificity of 'throw it in the river' (not just away — in the river) implies Tracy has thought about this before. Character-perfect dark absurdism.

jokes.text: Liz's party setup is described as looking like 'the post-coital suite at the NBA All-Star game'
jokes.setup: Jenna arrives at Liz's party and surveys the scene
jokes.punchline: The visual description — post-coital NBA All-Star suite — implies Liz has decorated for maximum debauchery while also implying the party looks somehow wrong or excessive
jokes.explanation: Jenna's pop culture reference as insult is very well-constructed. The specificity of the NBA All-Star game (known for a particular reputation) makes the image vivid and funny. Good economy.

jokes.text: Someone starts singing '* Jimmy Crack Corn and I Don't Care *' into the microphone — Liz: 'What are you doing?' — 'Juice fast delirium, Liz.'
jokes.setup: Liz is about to make a toast at her own party
jokes.punchline: Someone (presumably Liz herself) starts singing a children's song into the microphone instead — caused by juice fast delirium
jokes.explanation: The juice fast callback pays off. 'Juice fast delirium' as a medical condition causing inappropriate folk song singing is a good absurdist beat. The choice of 'Jimmy Crack Corn' specifically is right — it's the most meaningless children's song.

jokes.text: Liz's toast devolves into revealing she knows about Thursday Night Thunder and demanding everyone go around the room and apologize to her
jokes.setup: Liz starts a toast at her own party, ostensibly to celebrate Cerie
jokes.punchline: The toast spirals into a public breakdown about being excluded, ending with 'let's all go around the room and apologize to me!' — the toast becomes a tribunal
jokes.explanation: This is Liz Lemon at peak cringe — the thing she was warned about (revenge party) comes true in real time. 'Now let's all go around the room and apologize to me!' is a perfect ending to the breakdown. Highly quotable and very character-specific. The journey from legitimate grievance to complete self-destruction is well-constructed.

jokes.text: Jenna says Liz is 'going wide' and tells everyone to 'go out the window. Save yourselves.'
jokes.setup: Liz is spiraling at the party
jokes.punchline: Jenna's stage direction — 'going wide' as a performance note on Liz's breakdown — and the casual evacuation instruction as if this is a known emergency protocol
jokes.explanation: Jenna using performance vocabulary ('going wide') for a real emotional crisis is perfect character comedy. 'Save yourselves' as an evacuation order for a party meltdown is a good escalation.

jokes.text: Liz: 'I may not have a real family, but I thought at least I had one at work, which is not what I wanted for myself, by the way.'
jokes.setup: Liz is in full breakdown at her party
jokes.punchline: The parenthetical 'which is not what I wanted for myself, by the way' — Liz disclaiming her own need for workplace family even while expressing it — is self-aware and pathetic in exactly the right way
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character lines. The self-correction mid-breakdown — defensive even while vulnerable — is perfectly Liz Lemon. The show understands her character exactly here: she needs connection but is too proud to admit it, so she disclaims it in real time while demonstrating it. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Liz: 'You think when I was a kid I dreamed of someday paying $1,200 for a karaoke machine to impress a bunch of pasty losers? And a professional singer, who's beautiful, but doesn't know it.'
jokes.setup: Liz is in full breakdown
jokes.punchline: The self-awareness — she knows these are 'pasty losers' — plus the addendum about Jenna ('beautiful, but doesn't know it') which is obviously not true of Jenna, and Liz's defensiveness is projected onto a compliment for Jenna
jokes.explanation: The $1,200 karaoke machine is a funny detail (expensive, specific, stupid). The Jenna aside ('beautiful, but doesn't know it') is a non-compliment that probably means the opposite. Good character integration for both Liz and Jenna.

jokes.text: Dog bursts into the party during the breakdown — chaos erupts — '[whimpering] I had nowhere else to go!'
jokes.setup: Liz's party has already devolved into a breakdown; Kenneth arrives being chased by Tracy Senior
jokes.punchline: The dog attack interrupts the emotional climax perfectly — Kenneth's whimpering 'I had nowhere else to go!' is the punchline, implying the dog chased him to this specific location
jokes.explanation: The convergence of the dog subplot and the party subplot is well-timed. The physical chaos escalation (breakdown + dog attack) is a solid structural joke. Kenneth's whimpered explanation is a good button.

jokes.text: Tracy (in collar) tries to leave for the party — gets shocked — 'Oh, my neck! My swan-like neck! Aah!'
jokes.setup: Tracy had the electric collar put on him to prevent him from going to Liz's party
jokes.punchline: 'My swan-like neck!' — Tracy's description of his own neck as swan-like while being electrocuted is perfectly vain and absurd. The two attempts with shocks before he pushes through.
jokes.explanation: 'Swan-like neck' is a brilliantly specific piece of Tracy Jordan vanity. Most people being shocked would not pause to describe their neck aesthetic. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Tracy gets through the fence and announces: 'I'm free. I can go anywhere I want... like Liz's party. Or one of those places where you skydive over a huge fan.'
jokes.setup: Tracy has broken through the electric fence — declaring his freedom
jokes.punchline: The options Tracy considers with his new freedom: Liz's party OR 'one of those places where you skydive over a huge fan' — the second option is presented as equally valid and also implies it's a known type of establishment
jokes.explanation: The indoor skydiving reference as a random freedom-destination, presented as equivalent to a friend's party, is perfect Tracy. 'Those places' implies familiarity with a niche business. The freedom speech landing on a mundane choice (Liz's party) before the absurd alternative is good structure. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Tracy emerges on the other side of the fence: 'I'm free. I can go anywhere I want... like Liz's party or one of those places where you skydive over a huge fan.'
jokes.setup: Tracy triumphantly crosses the fence boundary
jokes.punchline: His celebration of freedom includes a mundane option (Liz's party) and a completely unhinged alternative (indoor skydiving over a fan) — the second option suggests his priorities
jokes.explanation: A nice beat. The choice of 'one of those places where you skydive over a huge fan' as an equally valid option to Liz's party is very Tracy — his idea of freedom is genuinely strange. The specificity of the description (it's indoor skydiving but described obliquely) is a good absurdist detail.

jokes.text: Tracy reaches Liz's building, tests the fence — seems to not work — 'Maybe it doesn't work on people any...' — gets shocked again — 'Aah! It still does!'
jokes.setup: Tracy is outside Liz's building — he tests the collar range
jokes.punchline: The fake-out — it seems to not work — then the immediate second shock proves it does. The callback to the collar gag continues.
jokes.explanation: Standard physical comedy fake-out. The construction is solid but not inventive. Works as escalation on the physical gag.

jokes.text: Party guests trapped by dog: 'You make us show up, you start yelling, and then we get attacked by a dog!' / 'And Cerie didn't even come. That's just a cardboard cutout of her.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is trapped in a room with a dog after Liz's party meltdown
jokes.punchline: The multi-item grievance list (show up → yelling → dog attack) is capped by the reveal that Cerie never came — she sent a cardboard cutout — which Liz apparently 'rescued' thinking it was real
jokes.explanation: The cardboard Cerie is a great visual gag. Cerie sending a cardboard cutout to her own work bridal shower is perfect for her character — she knew it would be bad and planned accordingly. 'But I rescued her' from Liz is a beautiful beat — implying Liz heroically dragged a piece of cardboard to safety. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: 'There's no fire escape in this room! Why are we even here? You make us show up, you start yelling, and then we get attacked by a dog!'
jokes.setup: Everyone is trapped and panicking from the dog
jokes.punchline: Someone's summary of the evening — including the bizarre specific grievance 'no fire escape' — is both a reasonable complaint and a perfect encapsulation of Liz's failed party
jokes.explanation: The list of complaints — show up, yelling, dog attack — is a nice summary of the episode's arc. Competent, funny in context.

jokes.text: 'And Cerie didn't even come. That's just a cardboard cutout of her.'
jokes.setup: The staff complains about the party; someone notes Cerie isn't there
jokes.punchline: Cerie was never there — what's been there all along is a cardboard cutout of her, apparently so realistic (or she's so two-dimensional) that no one noticed
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The cardboard cutout reveals two things simultaneously: (1) Cerie couldn't be bothered to attend her own work party; (2) She's so ornamental and two-dimensional as a character that a cardboard cutout is functionally equivalent. 'But I rescued her' — Liz apparently 'rescued' a cardboard cutout from the dog — adds a perfect button. Highly quotable, strong character integration, excellent economy.

jokes.text: Liz takes charge of the dog situation: 'Oh, really? Now I'm a part of the group?'
jokes.setup: The staff suddenly turns to Liz for leadership during the dog crisis
jokes.punchline: Liz clocks the irony — they only want her when there's a problem to solve
jokes.explanation: A solid character beat that articulates the episode's theme with some self-awareness. Good economy.

jokes.text: 'You know who's fun at parties? Paris Hilton, Andy Dick, Tracy — and they're all gonna burn in hell.'
jokes.setup: Coworker is defending Liz's lack of party fun
jokes.punchline: The list of 'fun' party people (Paris Hilton, Andy Dick, Tracy Jordan) all being destined for hell — the implication that fun = morally questionable
jokes.explanation: Good list joke. Paris Hilton and Andy Dick are expected; Tracy Jordan as the self-referential third member makes it show-specific and earns the laugh. The casual damnation as the punchline is sharp.

jokes.text: Someone prays: 'If you deliver me from this, I promise every Sunday for the rest of my life I'll go to... Pizza Hut. I'll go to Pizza Hut.'
jokes.setup: Someone trapped by the dog makes a desperate prayer/bargain with God
jokes.punchline: The prayer trails off implying a religious commitment — the pause builds expectation of 'church' — but delivers 'Pizza Hut'
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection construction. The pause ('...') is doing real work — we expect a church promise. 'Pizza Hut' lands because it's both the wrong answer and entirely believable as this character's version of a religious commitment. The repeat ('I'll go to Pizza Hut. Ha!') is a perfect button.

jokes.text: 'Look, if this is a family, that makes you the mom. And you don't want to go out drinking with your mom. You want mommy to make the monsters go away.'
jokes.setup: The coworker is explaining why they don't invite Liz to Thursday Night Thunder
jokes.punchline: Liz is the 'mom' of the workplace — not excluded but categorically different. The irony: Tracy warned her about this exact dynamic (parties/family) and now the dog attack is the 'monster' she has to solve
jokes.explanation: The thematic payoff of the episode. 'You want mommy to make the monsters go away' is the line that resolves Liz's arc — and immediately the literal dog monster needs to be dealt with. The structural double meaning (emotional resolution + plot trigger) earns 8+.

jokes.text: Liz faces down the dog — dramatic music — then gets attacked — 'Run! Run, my losers!'
jokes.setup: Liz has accepted her role as 'the mom' and steps up to deal with the dog
jokes.punchline: 'Run! Run, my losers!' — Liz's battle cry while being mauled, calling her co-workers 'my losers' as an affectionate term, the 'my' doing all the work
jokes.explanation: 'Run, my losers!' is an exceptional line. The 'my' transforms 'losers' from an insult to an endearment — Liz's complicated love for her staff expressed perfectly in extremis. It's also funny because she's being attacked while issuing the order. High quotability. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: 'Great party, Liz. Everybody take some cupcakes!'
jokes.setup: The party has descended into chaos — people running from a dog, Liz being mauled
jokes.punchline: Tracy arrives and cheerfully declares it a great party while instructing everyone to take cupcakes — completely ignoring the chaos, or perhaps finding it genuinely excellent
jokes.explanation: Tracy's oblivious enthusiasm for the disaster party is a good button. 'Everybody take some cupcakes!' implies Tracy brought cupcakes to a party he wasn't originally going to attend — the detail suggests he knew he'd end up there.

jokes.text: Jenna offers Jack one of her extra headshots to throw out — Subhas recoils: 'No! You're not book!' / Jenna: 'Why? What am I doing wrong?' / Subhas: 'Wanting to be book is not book.'
jokes.setup: Jenna offers a headshot — she's clearly trying to get into the janitors' 'special book'
jokes.punchline: Subhas rejects her because the very act of wanting to be in the book disqualifies her — 'wanting to be book is not book' — a Zen-like ruling on celebrity authenticity
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest jokes. 'Wanting to be book is not book' is a profound construction — it's simultaneously Zen wisdom and a very specific joke about Jenna's desperate celebrity ambition. The economy is perfect. It works as a comment on authenticity (you can't become cool by trying to be cool) AND as character comedy (Jenna is exactly the kind of person this rule was made for). Earns 8+ strongly.

jokes.text: 'So you solved your janitor thing. Now back to Nancy and Avery?' / 'Top Gun high-five for courage?' / 'Only because you look like you need it so badly. / I'm fine with that.'
jokes.setup: Jack has resolved the janitor situation and Liz is pushing him back toward his real problem
jokes.punchline: Jack proposing a 'Top Gun high-five for courage' — referencing the earlier mention — and Liz agreeing only because he clearly needs it, Jack accepting on those terms
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the Top Gun windmill high-five. Jack's need for physical validation via a movie reference and Liz's reluctant compliance is a sweet character beat. 'Only because you look like you need it so badly. / I'm fine with that.' is a good button.

tmdb_overview: Liz discovers that the TGS staff have been excluding her from their weekly hangouts, and strives to prove that she can be fun. Jack must choose between janitors and the shift time they both want, and Kenneth aids Tracy Jordan in being a good husband.
insight: Escalation comedy hits peak density with 2.89 jokes per minute across absurdist character bits.
